scope: Source-backed visual review cards for high-risk Chinese orchestra instrument artwork candidates.
policy: These cards are not approvals. They convert reference-source morphology into reviewer-facing acceptance and rejection tests. A candidate remains blocked until a professional reviewer confirms the card and import_approved_artwork.py --approve completes.
shared_thumbnail_tests: The instrument remains identifiable at App card size without relying on text labels.
The silhouette still shows the defining family: bowed huqin/gehu body, suona shawm profile, or sheng pipe-and-wind-chest profile.
No performer hand, decorative prop, lighting effect, or background shape hides the defining construction.
No visible callout, watermark, Chinese/English label, or fantasy marking appears inside the candidate image.

source_backed_features: Eason describes gehu as a lower-register Chinese orchestra instrument created to cover missing low bowed sounds.
Eason describes gehu as a hybrid between western cello and erhu, bowed like a cello.
Eason notes the gehu has body, bridge, spine, bow, and animal-skin-covered body.
The bass gehu / digehu relationship means the candidate must read as much larger than ordinary huqin entries.
acceptance_tests: Large vertical bowed body clearly reads as low-register instrument.
Body is not a plain western cello copy; it keeps Chinese bowed-instrument character.
Bridge, strings, long neck/spine, bow, and low support/endpin are plausible.
Body is visibly larger than zhonghu, erhu, gaohu, and banhu candidates.
At thumbnail size it reads as bass/low bowed Chinese orchestra instrument.
rejection_tests: Reject if the resonator is small like erhu, gaohu, banhu, or zhonghu.
Reject if the image is simply a western cello with no Chinese morphology.
Reject if it lacks bridge, strings, long vertical structure, or low support.
Reject if it looks like fantasy bass, viola da gamba, or electric cello.
Reject if scale does not clearly exceed zhonghu.
cards.reviewer_question: Would a Chinese orchestra bowed-string player identify this as gehu without reading the label?

source_backed_features: Grinnell identifies suona as a Chinese double-reed aerophone / shawm.
Grinnell describes a scalloped hardwood body with conical bore, seven fingerholes, one thumbhole, and a loosely attached flaring metal bell.
Grinnell describes a metal staple/bocal, pirouette disc, and small double reed at the top.
The Met notes suona varieties and the player's mouth covering the small reeds, reinforcing that it is not a brass trumpet.
acceptance_tests: Short conical wooden body is visible and not cylindrical.
Front finger holes are visible along the body.
Small double reed, staple/bocal, or pirouette area is visible at the top.
Loose flared metal bell is visually distinct from the wooden body.
Overall silhouette reads as shawm/laba/suona rather than brass.
rejection_tests: Reject if it has trumpet, bugle, or saxophone tubing.
Reject if it has a clarinet/oboe-like long straight western profile.
Reject if the whole instrument is metal.
Reject if the reed end and bell end are not distinguishable.
Reject if there are no finger holes.
cards.reviewer_question: Are reed, conical body, holes, and flared bell all credible enough for a suona player?

source_backed_features: Grinnell describes a free-reed aerophone with an incomplete circle of seventeen bamboo pipes.
Grinnell describes pipes mounted in a wooden bowl-shaped windchest with a short curved blowpipe.
Grinnell notes fingerholes around the circle of pipes just above the windchest.
Modernized sheng may add exterior resonator tubes, so the candidate may show traditional or modern pipe details if wind chest and mouthpiece remain clear.
acceptance_tests: Many vertical pipes of varied height dominate the silhouette.
Pipes are visibly inserted into a wind chest, bowl, or rounded air chamber.
A short curved or angled mouthpiece is attached to the wind chest.
Pipes are grouped as a Chinese mouth organ, not as a flat panpipe row.
Free-reed instrument identity is visible through pipe-and-wind-chest construction.
Wind chest and mouthpiece remain legible at thumbnail size.
rejection_tests: Reject if it looks like panpipes with no wind chest.
Reject if it resembles a pipe organ or bagpipe.
Reject if the pipes are random bamboo decoration not connected to an air chamber.
Reject if there is no visible blowpipe/mouthpiece.
Reject if the pipe cluster hides the wind chest entirely.
cards.reviewer_question: Does the image read as sheng, with pipes, wind chest, and mouthpiece all visible?

source_backed_features: Britannica describes banhu as a bowed Chinese fiddle and a type of huqin.
Britannica states its two strings stretch over a bamboo bridge resting on a wooden soundboard.
Britannica distinguishes banhu from most Chinese string instruments that use snakeskin membranes.
Britannica describes upright performance, bow passing between two strings, and semicircular resonator made of wood or coconut shell.
acceptance_tests: Vertical huqin-family form is clear.
Two strings and bow hair passing between strings are plausible.
Small resonator shows wooden soundboard identity rather than snakeskin erhu face.
Wood or coconut-shell body character is visible.
Candidate remains distinct from erhu, gaohu, zhonghu, and western violin.
rejection_tests: Reject if it is a standard snakeskin erhu with a different label.
Reject if the body is large like zhonghu or gehu.
Reject if it has a western violin/lute body.
Reject if wooden board or coconut-shell identity is absent.
Reject if bow/string geometry is impossible.
cards.reviewer_question: Could this pass as banhu to a huqin-family player without relying on the name label?

source_backed_features: The Met identifies erhu as a huqin; bow hairs pass between the strings and the instrument is played vertically on the knee.
The Met notes the erhu typically has a round or hexagonal sound box and a snakeskin belly.
Timbre and Orchestration identifies erhu as a core Chinese orchestra bowed string instrument.
Huqin construction includes wood soundbox, membrane, bridge, long thin neck, two tuning pegs, and bow fitted between strings.
acceptance_tests: Standard middle-size huqin vertical bowed form is clear.
Small round/hexagonal resonator with snakeskin membrane is visible.
Two strings, two pegs, bridge, long neck, and bow are plausible.
Bow hair appears between the strings rather than outside like a western violin bow.
It remains visually between smaller gaohu and larger zhonghu.
rejection_tests: Reject if the body is wooden-board banhu identity.
Reject if it is as small as gaohu or as large as zhonghu/gehu.
Reject if it looks like western violin/viola/cello.
Reject if bow hair is not between the strings.
Reject if no snakeskin/membrane resonator identity is visible.
cards.reviewer_question: Is this the neutral erhu reference image against which gaohu and zhonghu can be compared?

source_backed_features: Eason describes gaohu as higher-pitched than erhu and relatively smaller than erhu.
Eason associates gaohu with Cantonese music and soprano voicings in orchestra.
Timbre and Orchestration says gaohu is similar in construction to erhu, with orchestral versions often using baseplate/fabric like erhu and zhonghu.
Timbre and Orchestration states gaohu is tuned a fifth higher and has a smaller, more taut soundbox/membrane than erhu.
acceptance_tests: Small high-register huqin silhouette is visible.
Resonator is smaller and lighter than erhu candidate.
Two strings, bow hair between strings, pegs, and long neck are plausible.
Image implies brighter/soprano huqin role without needing a performer.
Candidate remains distinct from erhu and zhonghu in side-by-side review.
rejection_tests: Reject if it is the same size as erhu.
Reject if body is larger/lower like zhonghu.
Reject if it uses banhu wooden-board identity.
Reject if it turns into gehu or western violin family.
Reject if the high-register compact character is not visible.
cards.reviewer_question: If labels are removed, can a reviewer still see this as the smaller/higher gaohu?

source_backed_features: Eason states zhonghu is typically assigned the alto voice in the Chinese orchestra bowed string section.
Eason describes zhonghu as slightly bigger than erhu, with wood soundbox shapes ranging from circular to octagonal.
Eason describes zhonghu as middle-to-lower range with thick timbre and deep tone.
Timbre and Orchestration says zhonghu open strings are a fifth lower than erhu and that zhonghu has thicker strings and a larger body.
acceptance_tests: Larger lower-register huqin silhouette is clear.
Resonator body and neck are more robust than erhu and gaohu candidates.
Two strings, pegs, bridge, membrane/soundbox, and bow are plausible.
Image reads as alto/lower huqin, not bass gehu.
Candidate remains distinct from erhu in side-by-side review.
rejection_tests: Reject if it is the same size as erhu.
Reject if it is tiny like gaohu.
Reject if it becomes gehu/cello-sized.
Reject if it uses banhu wooden-board identity.
Reject if the body is not visibly larger than erhu.
cards.reviewer_question: Does the candidate clearly communicate zhonghu's larger, lower alto role without becoming gehu?
